progression.prerequisiteKnowledge: chem-m7-c04a (addition: two molecules make one, nothing lost; the weaker second bond of a C=C opens; the reagent splits, one piece on each carbon; conditions on the arrow; the four alkene additions and the conditions card; bromine water loses its colour when an alkene adds bromine; an unsymmetrical alkene can give two products; haloalkane naming with locants; "HBr as a second product would be substitution", c04a scene 9), chem-m7-c03 (tetrahedral, trigonal planar and linear carbons; a double bond's second bond is weaker and lies above and below the carbons; general formulas CnH2n+2, CnH2n, CnH2n−2), chem-m7-c01 (naming hydrocarbons, locants, di-; ethyne, propyne). Module 5: a catalyst speeds up a reaction and is not used up (chem-m5-c04b). Year 11: balancing equations; light as a form of energy. Not assumed: substitution reaction, UV light's role, "excess", alkyne addition, tetra-.
progression.startsWith: Recall addition from c04a; compare a saturated alkane. The video opens: Shake hex-one-ene with orange bromine water, and the colour disappears almost at once, even in the dark. That's the double bond adding bromine, from the last video. Now add bromine to hexane, an alkane.
progression.stopsAfter: explaining why an alkane does not add and needs UV light to react with a halogen; writing a substitution equation with UV light on the arrow and HX as the second product; explaining why UV light is not a catalyst; telling substitution from addition by the products; recognising that substitution gives a mixture; writing the two steps of alkyne addition with H₂, X₂ and HX, and the overall equation for excess reagent; naming the products; explaining what bromine water can and cannot show. No mechanism, no Markovnikov, no Lindlar, no alkyne hydration product, no test method (chem-m7-p02).
progression.nextLesson: testing hydrocarbons with bromine water in the lab (route chem-m7-p02, "Test unsaturation with bromine water").

teaching.task: Hexane and hex-1-ene both meet bromine, but only the alkene reacts in the dark, and when the alkane finally reacts under UV light, it gives off hydrogen bromide too. Why do alkanes substitute while alkenes and alkynes add, and what does each make?
teaching.causalExplanation: (1) an alkane can react with bromine, but only with UV light, and it makes an extra gas (1); (2) an alkane has only strong single bonds and no spare bond, so nothing can add, and a bond must break first, which takes energy (2); (3) UV light supplies that energy; the result is a swap; the swapped-out hydrogen leaves with the other bromine as HBr (3); (4) UV light is energy, not a substance, and it is absorbed, so it is not a catalyst; it goes on the arrow; an alkene needs no light (4); (5) one product means addition, two products with HX means substitution; the model shows the carbon stays tetrahedral (5); (6) substitution can repeat and can happen at different carbons, so it gives a mixture (6); (7) a triple bond has two weaker extra bonds, so an alkyne adds twice, one piece on each carbon each time; the model goes linear, flat, tetrahedral (7); (8) how much reagent decides the step: hydrogen goes to ethene then ethane; excess means both steps; HBr gives bromoethene, then a second HBr adds in the same way (8); (9) water adds too but its product changes family; alkenes and alkynes both decolourise bromine water because both add, alkanes do not, so for an open-chain hydrocarbon with one multiple bond the formula decides which (9); memory aid (10); two attempts and brief feedback (11 to 14); handoff (15); key notes (16).
teaching.conversationalApproach: hex-1-ene decolourises bromine water at once even in the dark, while hexane stays orange until UV light shines on it and hydrogen bromide fumes come off, so the video asks why alkanes need the light and where the hydrogen bromide comes from. An alkane has only strong single bonds and no spare bond, so a bond has to break first; UV light supplies the energy to split bromine molecules and start a swap in which one hydrogen is replaced by a bromine and leaves as HBr, a substitution with two products. UV light goes on the arrow as an energy source, not a catalyst, because it is not a substance and is absorbed. Addition and substitution are set side by side (one product against two, flat carbons turning tetrahedral against carbons that stay tetrahedral), substitution is shown to continue to tetrachloromethane and to happen at different carbons, so it usually gives a mixture. An alkyne's two extra bonds let it add twice, with the amount of reagent deciding the step and excess meaning both steps; water and alkynes are left for later, and bromine water shows unsaturation but not which kind, so for an open-chain hydrocarbon with one multiple bond the formula decides. The memory aid is alkanes swap, alkenes add, alkynes add twice. Two exam questions follow with brief feedback.
teaching.openingDecision: Shake hex-one-ene with orange bromine water, and the colour disappears almost at once, even in the dark. That's the double bond adding bromine, from the last video. Now add bromine to hexane, an alkane. In the dark, the orange stays. Shine UV light on it, though, and the colour slowly fades, and fumes of hydrogen bromide come off. So alkanes can react with bromine after all. Why do they need the light, and where does that hydrogen bromide come from?
teaching.understandingCheck: (A1) "Propane reacts with chlorine gas in the presence of UV light. Identify the type of reaction, and write a balanced equation, using structural formulae, for the formation of one organic product." New alkane and halogen pairing (the scenes use ethane and bromine; propane appears in scene 6 only as two names); tests the substitution pattern, the HCl second product and "one organic product" from a mixture. Crossed mistake: "CH₃CH₂CH₃ + Cl₂ → CH₃CH₂CH₂Cl" (no HCl; the atoms do not balance). This is the mirror of c04a's crossed mistake (HCl wrongly written in an addition). (A2) "Propyne, CH₃C≡CH, reacts with excess bromine at room temperature. Explain why each molecule of propyne reacts with two molecules of bromine, and name the final organic product." New alkyne (scenes use ethyne; the site worked example uses but-2-yne); tests the two extra bonds, "excess" and tetrabromo naming with locants. Crossed mistake: "1,2-dibromoprop-1-ene" (stopping after one step; site lesson 8 Error 6 pattern).
teaching.curriculumScope: Syllabus (NSW Chemistry Stage 6, 2017), as printed: "investigate, write equations and construct models to represent the reactions of unsaturated hydrocarbons when added to a range of chemicals, including but not limited to:; hydrogen (H2); halogens (X2); hydrogen halides (HX); water (H2O) (ACSCH136)" "investigate, write equations and construct models to represent the reactions of saturated hydrocarbons when substituted with halogens" This part covers alkynes for the first dotpoint (alkenes were chem-m7-c04a) and all of the second. this video starts by recalling addition from chem-m7-c04a and comparing it with a saturated alkane, and stops at predicting the products and conditions of alkane substitution and alkyne addition. It teaches: an alkane does not react with bromine in the dark at room temperature, because it has only strong single bonds and no spare bond to open; UV light supplies the energy to start the reaction (by splitting halogen molecules, one clause only); the overall result is a substitution, one hydrogen swapped for a halogen, with the hydrogen leaving as HX, the second product (ethane and bromine); the carbon keeps four single bonds and stays tetrahedral (one ink ball-and-stick model); UV light goes on the arrow and is an energy source, not a catalyst (Module 5 callback: a catalyst is a substance that is not used up); addition against substitution by counting products (one, or two with HX); substitution can continue (methane to tetrachloromethane, screen chain only) and can happen at different carbons (propane gives 1-chloropropane or 2-chloropropane), so it gives a mixture; a triple bond has two weaker extra bonds (c03 callback), so an alkyne adds twice, one piece on each carbon each time (ethyne and bromine: 1,2-dibromoethene, then 1,1,2,2-tetrabromoethane; the model goes linear, then flat, then tetrahedral); ethyne with hydrogen and a nickel catalyst becomes ethene, then ethane (overall + 2H₂); "excess" means go to the second step; ethyne and HBr give bromoethene, then a dibromoethane (a second HBr adds in the same way; only 1,1-dibromoethane is shown, not labelled major); water adds to alkynes too, but its product rearranges into a family met later (one sentence, no product); alkenes and alkynes both decolourise bromine water at room temperature without UV light, alkanes do not, so the test shows a multiple bond but not which one, and for an open-chain hydrocarbon with one multiple bond the molecular formula decides (c03 general formulas). Not here: the four alkene additions and their conditions (chem-m7-c04a; recalled once with the conditions card); the bromine water test method, safety and observations (chem-m7-p02, the next video); the free radical chain mechanism (initiation, propagation, termination; see Decisions); Markovnikov's rule and which dibromoethane forms more (author note e); partial hydrogenation with the Lindlar catalyst, cis alkenes (site extension); alkyne hydration products, enols and ketones (site extension; ketones are chem-m7-c08b); the "two portions of bromine water" test (correction 4); combustion and its balancing (site lesson 7 card 4; alcohol combustion is chem-m7-c07; author note h); haloalkane reactions (chem-m7-c13); polymerisation (chem-m7-c14); geminal and vicinal as terms.

design.visualSystem: Explainer engine: warm paper stage, handwritten Caveat headings, amber doodle layer. Colour key as chem-m7-c01 to c04a: carbon skeleton ink; hydrogens soft grey; the C=C and C≡C teal, their weaker extra bonds shown as teal clouds; bromine deep orange-brown; chlorine green; new atoms from the reagent keep their colour in the product; condition chips navy on the arrow, except "UV light", which is violet; the swapped-out H bright grey; the HX second product boxed in thin violet. Board layout (constant): top-left the short task chip ("Alkane + Br₂", "Alkyne: step 1 of 2"); centre the equation stage strip (or the two-step strip), one equation at a time; the product counter under it; c04a's conditions card small at the right from scene 4; plates small at the left or right only in scenes 1, 4 and 9. Clutter rule: at most three text items bright at once; every label fades when its sentence ends; the previous equation leaves before the next one draws. Reuse: painted plates (inspected 22 Oct): `m7-bromine-water-orange-v1.png` and `m7-bromine-water-colourless-v1.png` (the matched before and after tubes; 2000 × 2000), cross-faded in place in the hook for hex-1-ene; `m7-bromine-water-pair-v1.png` (the two tubes side by side; 2000 × 2000) in scene 9. All scale uniformly only, never stretched. New plates: `m7-bromine-hexane-orange-v1.png`, `m7-bromine-hexane-faded-v1.png` and `m7-uv-lamp-v1.png` (hook and scene 4); see Assets. No human figures.
